requested_changes.body: Need to double-check that the malloc-ed size of `work` is large enough for the intended use of `ab`, which is `(2*ku + kl + 1) * n` IIUC. This limits the usable values of kl and ku?
This needs to handle the case of `info < 0`, too:  cf https://www.netlib.org/lapack/explore-html/db/df8/group__gbsv_gaff55317eb3aed2278a85919a488fec07.html#gaff55317eb3aed2278a85919a488fec07

This is new relative to to main (which skips "banded" in the structure structure detection), and it goes against @ilayn's suggestion at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/23774#issuecomment-3631006935

The rest of `solve` mainly follows Matlab's mldivide, cf the "dense inputs" block-scheme in https://www.mathworks.com/help/matlab/ref/double.mldivide.html which does not have "banded"

So this probably needs to be removed in the end. Meanwhile I'm curious what the performance characteristics are for few bands (e.g. N=100 and n_bands=5). So could you
- add  a benchmark to https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/main/benchmarks/benchmarks/linalg.py#L105
- run it with `$ spin bench --compare main -t BatchedSolveBench` and report the results here
- remove this in a separate commit to simplify further experimentation.
Minor nit: `free(NULL)` is a no-op, so there's no need to `if (kls != NULL)`.
Nit: it's generally better to fix some explicit tolerance, `atol=1e-14` essentially says "equal in floating point modulo some modest error accumulation"

requested_changes.body:
This is a strange place to branch into `_solve_assume_banded`, in a middle of the `lwork` computation.
Please move the branching to happen earlier. 
Also, it might be cleaner if `_solve_assume_banded` received a pair of `PyArrayObject *`s instead of 17 positional arguments, the majority of which are derived from said `PyArrayObject *`s.

Could you please roll back this change? It is unrelated to the banded solver, so let's keep the scope.

We had a discussion with @ilayn several months ago about this part, and IIRC and IIUC @ilayn's statement is that this two-step copy-then-transpose can be faster than a single-step `copy_to_F_order`. My quick-and-dirty testing seemed to indicate that the latter is actually faster, but I did not do any systematic investigation. So let's keep it for a separate PR/issue/discussion (and make sure it includes Ilhan).

Normalizing the strides? 
To check my understanding: this receives a dense strided array in `data` with the size of `n`-by-`n`, and strides `s1` and `s2`, and extracts `kl + ku + 1` diagonals into a pre-allocated banded storage of size `ldab`-by-`n`; Also, it cannot receive the original numpy array because it only operates on a single 2D slice. Is this correct?
Please tweak the "normalize the strides" comment if so.
